hints: Look closely at what happens to the ethene molecule, especially its carbon-carbon double bond.
Notice that two reactant molecules, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, combine to form just one single product.
Think about which reaction type adds atoms across a C=C double bond and turns an alkene into a single saturated product.
walkthrough:
**Spot the key functional group**

Look at the starting organic molecule. Ethene, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$, is an alkene with a C=C double bond. That double bond is electron rich and loves to react.

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$

**See what adds across the double bond**

In the product, ethanol, the double bond is gone. An H atom has added to one carbon and an OH group has added to the other carbon. Nothing is lost or replaced.

Addition across C=C: $\text{C=C} + \text{H-OH} \rightarrow \text{H-C-C-OH}$

**Name the reaction type**

When two molecules join together to make one bigger molecule, with the pi bond breaking, we call it addition. Here water adds to ethene, so this is hydration by electrophilic addition. Sulfuric acid is just the catalyst.

options.A: Not correct. Although sulfuric acid is present, it acts as a catalyst and is not neutralised. There is no base forming a salt and water, so this is not an acid-base reaction.
options.B: Correct. Two molecules combine into one product with loss of unsaturation. The H and OH from water add across the C=C double bond of ethene to give ethanol. This is the classic hydration of an alkene, an electrophilic addition reaction.
options.C: Not correct. Hydrolysis uses water to split one molecule into two smaller molecules, for example an ester into acid plus alcohol. Here the opposite happens, two molecules join into one, so it is addition, not hydrolysis.
options.D: Not correct. In substitution one atom or group is swapped for another, with a leaving group lost. Here nothing leaves ethene, atoms are only added across the double bond.
